analysis.statement:
## Refresh temporally activated package-backed references

Implement `refresh_references(initial, snapshots, references)` and return one tuple per reference, in input order:

`(status, namespace, location, hash)`

`status` is `"invalid"`, `"missing"`, or `"located"`.

The initial index is snapshot 0. Applying atomic batch `i` produces snapshot `i`. An entry has `namespace`, `name`, `version`, and nonempty opaque `hash`. An update has the same fields, but `hash=None` deletes its key. A key is `(namespace, name, version)`. Keys are unique within `initial` and within each batch. Namespaces are `"type"`, `"function"`, and `"value"`. Names are canonical dot-separated fully qualified names. Type versions are `None`; function/value versions are `None` or integers.

A reference has `namespace`, `text`, `context`, `location`, `hash`, and `start`. `start` is an integer from 0 through `len(snapshots)`: the reference does not exist before that snapshot and is processed at `start` and every later snapshot. If `location` is `None`, `hash` is also `None`; otherwise both are canonical and nonempty respectively.

Identifiers contain only ASCII letters, digits, or `_`. Module identifiers and functio
constraints: All non-reference input obeys its canonical rules. There are at most 200,000 snapshots, entries, updates, and references each, and at most 1,000,000 induced candidate names. Use only the standard library, with no I/O or global state.
time_memory_risks: numeric bounds too large for naive loops or arrays
n up to ~1e5–5e5; need near-linear work

plan.approach: Write a direct Python implementation of the stated rules. Never loop or allocate using a 1e9/1e18 bound; iterate input size only. Prefer maps, difference arrays, or lazy simulation.
